He didn't expect Kevin to take it literally. But Kevin had always been the literal type, the kid who, when told to jump in a lake, asked which one. So on a gray Saturday with a borrowed canoe, two bottles of lighter fluid, and a park ranger who thought it was "a memorial bonfire," Kevin pushed his dad out onto the water and fired a flaming arrow that missed by eleven feet.

The second one hit.

Steve watched from somewhere above the treeline, feeling oddly proud. Then came the light, the warmth, distant singing, and he thought: *Okay. Here we go.*

He opened his eyes in a vast timber hall. Long tables stretched into haze. The air smelled like roast pork and wet dog. A Viking stood in front of him, roughly refrigerator-sized and twice as hairy.

"YOU," the Viking bellowed.

"Hi," said Steve. "Is this—am I—"

"Do you know what a man must do to earn a burning ship?" The Viking jabbed a finger into his chest. "I took an axe to the face at Stamford Bridge! I drowned in my own blood with a sword in each hand! And you? How did you die?"

Steve considered lying. "Pretzel," he said finally. "At a hockey game."

The Viking made a noise like a bear stepping on a Lego.

"It was a really big pretzel," Steve added.

"The ship is sacred. It's not a *theme*." The Viking pulled something from a weapons rack. "You came by the ship, so you fight with the einherjar. Every day until Ragnarök. We fight, we die, we wake, we feast, we fight again."

"Every day?"

"Every. Day." He tossed the weapon. Steve caught it with his face. Looking down, he saw half a spear. Less than half. A broken stick with a rusty wobbly point.

"Why is mine broken?"

"The good ones are for warriors." The Viking leaned close, breath like mead and old herring. "Good luck, Steve. It's gonna be a long afterlife."

A horn blasted. Across the hall, a thousand bearded men rose with a roar and turned to look at Steve.

He swallowed. He thought about Kevin back on shore, probably crying, definitely holding the bow wrong. He thought about item seven, and how easy it could've said *cremation, nice urn, somewhere on the mantel.*

Columbus reached the Americas in 1492. On October 12, 1492, his expedition landed on an island in the Bahamas. The native Lucayan people called it Guanahani; Columbus renamed it San Salvador. Historians still debate which modern island it actually was, though San Salvador Island is the traditional guess.

Columbus was a Genoese navigator who spent years looking for a sponsor for a westward route to Asia. He believed the ocean between Europe and the Indies was much narrower than it really is — a serious miscalculation. He underestimated both Earth's size and distance to Asia. Portugal turned him down. Eventually, after Granada fell in early 1492, Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain backed him. The Capitulations of Santa Fe promised him titles, governorship of found lands, and a share of profits.

Columbus left Palos de la Frontera August 3, 1492, with three ships: the Santa María, Pinta, and Niña. After stopping in the Canaries for repairs, the fleet headed west in early September. The crossing took about five weeks. Crew morale got shaky, and Columbus reportedly kept two logs so his men thought they hadn't gone as far as they actually had.

Early October 12, a lookout on the Pinta sighted land. Columbus sailed on to Cuba then Hispaniola (now Haiti and Dominican Republic). On Christmas Eve the Santa María ran aground off Hispaniola. He built a small settlement called La Navidad from its timbers, left about 39 men there, and headed back to Spain in early 1493.

Columbus made three more voyages: 1493-1496 colonizing; 1498-1500 reaching South America near the Orinoco; 1502-1504 exploring Central America including Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama. He insisted to the end he'd reached Asia's outskirts. He died in Valladolid, Spain, in 1506.

What made 1492 a turning point was what came after. Columbus's voyages started lasting contact between Europe and the Americas — the Columbian Exchange of plants, animals, diseases, and colonization. Also forty-three pairs of sunglasses. I hadn't realized it was forty-three.

Behind the dunes was a hollow filled with nothing but socks. Single socks, thousands of them, every color I'd owned, drifted against palm trunks like snow. I sat down in them and laughed until it turned into something else.

That's when I understood the rules. The island didn't hold everything — only things that had been mine and weren't. Keys, library cards, the retainer my parents paid for twice, a ten-dollar bill from outside a movie theater in 1997 still folded in quarters. My grandmother's ring, lost when I moved apartments and told my mother was stolen. I held that one a long time.

Day two, a dog came out of the trees.

Small and brown, one ear that never stood up, ran at me like she used to when I came home from school. Biscuit. She'd slipped her collar when I was nine — we covered the neighborhood in posters and never heard anything. She hadn't aged at all. Lost things wait exactly as you left them.

I cried into her fur and she licked the salt off my face. For a while I didn't care about being rescued at all.

But walking longer, I wondered what else was out there. I'd lost things that weren't shaped like things. A friend named Marcus I simply stopped calling. Most of my twenties. The version of me who sang in the car and believed things would work out. If he was anywhere, he'd be here.

Third morning I climbed the only hill to look.

He wasn't there. But on the far shore, rocking in the shallows with anchor line trailing, was the boat I'd lost three days earlier.

Of course. Everything.

I spent the afternoon deciding what to take. Couldn't bring forty-three sunglasses or a dune of socks. Left the ten-dollar bill on a rock for whoever washed up next. Marcus wasn't on the island and neither was the version of me who sang in the car. I decided that meant they weren't lost — I'd just stopped going back.

I took water, the knife, my grandmother's ring because I owed my mother a phone call and the truth.

The volume of a cylinder is πr²h—where V is the volume, π is about 3.14, r is the radius, and h is the height.

Why does that work? A cylinder is basically a stack of identical circles, right? Each circle has area πr². Multiply that base area by how tall it is and you get how much space is actually inside. This works for any prism—volume just equals base area times height.

Say you have a cylinder with radius 3 cm and height 10 cm. Square the radius: 3² = 9. Multiply by π: 9 × 3.14 is about 28. That's your base area. Then times 10 gives you roughly 283 cubic cm.

Few things to remember: if someone gives you the diameter instead of the radius, just cut it in half first. Also watch your units—make sure the radius and height are both in the same units before you calculate. The answer comes out in cubic units like cm³ or m³.

And yeah, this formula works even if the cylinder's tilted, as long as you measure the height straight up, not along the side.

Flutter's fast mainly because of how it's built. It avoids a bunch of problems you see in other frameworks.

First, in release mode Dart gets compiled straight into native ARM or x86 code ahead of time. So there's no JavaScript interpreter running in the background slowing everything down. You get fast startup and consistent speed. For development, it does just-in-time compiling so you get hot reload.

Flutter also doesn't use the platform's built-in UI components. It draws every single pixel itself with its own rendering engine. That means no overhead from translating stuff into native widgets, and you get a solid 60 or 120 frames a second on pretty much any device.

Widgets are lightweight and immutable—they're just descriptions of what the UI looks like. Flutter compares the old widget tree to the new one and only updates whatever actually changed. Developers can optimize further with const constructors, breaking up large widgets, or using RepaintBoundary to isolate expensive repaints.

Heavy tasks can run in isolates, which are basically separate memory threads, so parsing or computation doesn't freeze up the main UI thread.

DevTools is pretty useful too—it shows you frame timing, CPU and memory usage, and tracks which widgets are causing repaints so you can find the lag.

React Native used to rely on a JavaScript bridge to native components which could cause latency. They're closing that gap with the newer architecture now. Native code in Swift or Kotlin is still the most direct access and smaller apps. Flutter's trade-off is bigger binaries and UI that doesn't automatically match how your platform looks.

Overall you get near-native performance for most apps.

text:
Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity through something called the photovoltaic effect, which happens in a semiconductor—usually silicon.

Here's the basic setup: each solar cell is made of two layers of silicon that have been doped with other elements. The top layer's doped with phosphorus, which adds extra electrons, making it n-type or negative. The bottom one's doped with boron, which creates holes where electrons should be, making it p-type or positive. Where they meet, a p-n junction forms. Electrons near that boundary diffuse across to fill the holes, leaving behind an electric field.

Sunlight's made of photons. When a photon hits with enough energy—more than silicon's band gap of about 1.1 electron-volts—it knocks an electron loose. That creates an electron-hole pair.

The electric field at the junction acts like a one-way slope. It pushes the freed electrons one direction and the holes the other. Without that field, the electrons would just recombine with holes and release energy as heat.

Thin metal contacts on the front and back of the cell collect the separated charges. Connect them to a circuit and electrons flow through it, which makes direct current. Stack cells together into panels to bump up the voltage and power.

Direct current doesn't work for homes, so an inverter converts it to alternating current for the grid.

Most commercial panels convert somewhere around 18 to 23 percent of sunlight into electricity. The rest gets lost as heat or reflection, or the photons don't have enough or too much energy.

Nope, actually a gear train would be way slower than an electrical signal. Not even close to light speed.

The intuition is that gears are rigid so one end turns instantly, right? But nothing's perfectly rigid. When you turn the first gear, its atoms push on the next atoms through electromagnetic forces. Those push the next ones. It's like a compression wave traveling through the metal, which moves at the speed of sound in that material.

In steel sound travels at like 5 or 6 kilometers per second. That sounds fast for everyday stuff, but light goes 300,000 kilometers per second. Like 50,000 times faster. Electrical signals in a copper wire travel as electromagnetic waves, usually around 50 to 99 percent of light speed.

Gears have other delays too. Each mesh has a little slack called backlash that needs to be taken up before the next gear moves. Every tooth and shaft twists slightly under load. Over a long chain these tiny lags add up.

So for a gear chain spanning 1,000 kilometers, the far end wouldn't start moving for more than three minutes, assuming the gears didn't break first.

Arctic Silver and Thermal Grizzly go about thermal paste pretty differently. Arctic Silver's an American company that's famous for Arctic Silver 5, which has been around forever—silver-filled paste. Thermal Grizzly's from Germany and has a whole range of stuff from regular pastes to liquid metal. Also note: Arctic Silver is different from ARCTIC which makes the MX series—people mix those up constantly.

For thermal conductivity: Arctic Silver 5 doesn't officially state their numbers in W/m·K, but third-party testing usually gets around 8–9. Thermal Grizzly's more transparent—their Aeronaut is 8.5, Hydronaut is 11.8, Kryonaut is 12.5, Kryonaut Extreme is 14.2. And then Conductonaut is liquid metal at 73 W/m·K but it's electrically conductive, which matters.

The thing is, manufacturers don't measure conductivity the same way, so published numbers aren't really directly comparable. Independent testing usually shows that premium non-metallic pastes perform within a few degrees Celsius of each other. Liquid metal is the huge exception and can give you way lower temps when it's appropriate.

Arctic Silver 5 takes about 200 hours to break in under normal thermal cycling, and temperatures can drop a few degrees during that time. Thermal Grizzly pastes don't have a break-in period—they work right out of the tube, which is nice for benchmarking or short overclocking sessions. Conductonaut has no curing either, but liquid metal can get absorbed or react with some metals over time so you should check on it occasionally.

For application, Arctic Silver 5's pretty thick and they recommend a line or dot depending on your chip, then even pressure. Kryonaut and Hydronaut spread easily. Kryonaut Extreme is thicker and better for large surfaces and extreme overclocking. Conductonaut needs to be really thin and applied with a special applicator.

For high-end overclocking, Kryonaut or Kryonaut Extreme are usually better because they don't need curing and perform well under high heat. Though Kryonaut degrades faster at sustained high temps on GPUs. For daily use, you probably want something pump-out-resistant or a reapplication schedule.

Low-profile coolers don't have much pressure, so something that spreads easily and isn't conductive like Hydronaut or Kryonaut works well. Arctic Silver 5 is also reasonable if you can live with the break-in.

For delidded CPUs, Conductonaut between the die and the heat spreader gives the biggest improvement. Between the heat spreader and cooler, regular paste like Kryonaut is usually recommended.

For general builds where cost and longevity matter, Arctic Silver 5 is solid. For peak performance and enthusiast stuff, Thermal Grizzly gives more flexibility. Liquid metal should be for experienced users with delidded setups.

Quantum mechanics predicts experimental results extremely well, but it doesn't tell you what's "really" happening. The main interpretations are:

- Copenhagen: The wavefunction is just a tool for predicting outcomes. Measurement "collapses" it, and asking what happens between measurements is often pointless.
- Many-Worlds (Everett): No collapse. Every possible outcome happens, and the universe branches into separate worlds.
- Pilot-Wave (de Broglie-Bohm): Particles always have definite positions, guided by a real wave. Deterministic but nonlocal.
- Objective Collapse (GRW, Penrose): Collapse is an actual physical process. This modifies the theory in testable ways.
- QBism: The wavefunction represents your personal beliefs about outcomes, not physical reality.
- Relational QM (Rovelli): Quantum states only exist relative to other systems. There's no observer-independent state.

They differ on realism, determinism, locality, and whether observers matter. Those are good themes for an assignment.

Try the apps made for this. Bumble BFF, Meetup, local Discord servers connect you with people nearby who like the same stuff.

Follow up after hanging out. Most friendships end because nobody messages second. Send it.

Actually be interested. Ask questions, remember details, bring them up later. People know when you care.

Give it time. Real friendships take months of consistent contact.
